a: him
p: The speaker is the heavenly messenger of chapter 10. "Him" is Darius in the Hebrew, but the sense is debated.
b: The long speech of chapters 11-12 comes from the figure who has been talking to Daniel since 10:10-21. He says he stood beside "him" in Darius' first year. In 10:21 the only one who stands firm with the messenger against the princes of Persia and Greece is Michael, so some readers take "him" to be Michael (Jerome and many others). Others take "him" to be Darius the Mede: heaven backed the new king who would let the exiles go. The Hebrew allows both. "Darius the Mede" is itself a puzzle (see 9:1 and 5:31); the Greek solves it by reading "Cyrus" (see the variant). The Plain keeps the Hebrew and leaves "him" open.

a: Three more kings are about to rise for Persia
p: Four Persian kings are named only by number. Persia's last 200 years are packed into this verse.
b: Most readers count Cambyses (530-522 BC), a usurper called Bardiya or Smerdis (522 BC) and Darius I (522-486 BC) as the three, and Xerxes I (486-465 BC) as the fourth. Xerxes' vast wealth and his huge invasion of Greece in 480-479 BC fit "he will call everyone to arms against the kingdom of Greece" (Jerome gives this count). Defenders of a sixth-century date say the angel names only the kings who mattered to the Greek conflict. Critical scholars see the jump from Xerxes to Alexander as a sign that the author knew the Persian period only in outline. Other counts exist; the Hebrew gives no names.

a: a powerful king
p: Almost every reader takes the powerful king to be Alexander, who died in 323 BC.
b: The "powerful king" with a "vast realm" is Alexander of Macedon (336-323 BC), who overthrew the Persian Empire. This is the same figure as the goat's great horn in Daniel 8:5-8, 21. Jews of later centuries told stories about Alexander at Jerusalem; Josephus says the book of Daniel was shown to him there (Antiquities 11.8.5), a story historians doubt. Defenders of a sixth-century date read it as prophecy, critics as history written as prophecy; both agree the verse describes Alexander.

a: shared out among the four winds of the sky
p: Alexander's heirs were killed and his generals divided his empire. The text sees four parts.
b: Alexander died young in 323 BC. His half-brother Philip III Arrhidaeus and his infant son Alexander IV were both murdered (317 and about 310 BC), so "his offspring" never ruled. His generals, the Diadochi ("successors"), fought for forty years. After the battle of Ipsus in 301 BC four kingdoms stood: Cassander in Macedonia, Lysimachus in Thrace and Asia Minor, Seleucus in Syria and the east, and Ptolemy in Egypt. Daniel 8:8, 22 also speaks of four horns. "The four winds of the sky" is a figure for every direction (Daniel 7:2; Zechariah 2:6). The text then follows only two of the four, the ones that held Judea between them.

a: The king of the south
t: South and north: the Ptolemies and the Seleucids
p: "South" and "north" are Egypt and Syria, named from Judea's point of view.
b: The directions are seen from Judea. The king of the south is the Ptolemaic king of Egypt; the king of the north is the Seleucid king in Syria and the lands east of it. Judea sat on the road between them and changed hands several times. Here the king of the south is Ptolemy I Soter (about 305-282 BC), and his "commander" who grew stronger is Seleucus I Nicator (died 281 BC), who had served Ptolemy and then built the larger realm. The whole survey to 11:20 runs on this pattern: a king of one side, a marriage or a war, a successor. Ancient historians who tell the same events include Polybius and Appian (Syrian Wars); 1 Maccabees 1:1-10 gives the Jewish summary.

a: The daughter of the king of the south will go to the king of the north
p: About 252 BC Ptolemy II sent his daughter Berenice to marry Antiochus II. It ended in murder.
b: Ptolemy II Philadelphus (285-246 BC) gave his daughter Berenice to Antiochus II Theos (261-246 BC), who had to set aside his first wife Laodice. Antiochus died in 246 BC, probably poisoned by Laodice, who also had Berenice, her baby son and her Egyptian attendants killed. The verse's pairs "she, those who brought her, the one who fathered her, the one who backed her" read as her escort, her father (who had died shortly before) and her husband or supporter. The Hebrew text of two phrases is uncertain (see the two variants beside this verse). The Plain follows the Masoretic pointing.

a: a shoot from her own roots
p: Her brother Ptolemy III Euergetes took revenge in the Third Syrian War, 246-241 BC.
b: The "branch from the same roots" is her brother, Ptolemy III Euergetes (246-222 BC). He invaded Syria in the Third Syrian War (the "Laodicean War", 246-241 BC) and overran much of the Seleucid coast. Verse 9 is read of Seleucus II Callinicus, who about 242 BC tried to take back what Ptolemy had won. He regained some cities in Syria, was then defeated, and lost his fleet in a storm (Justin 27.2). The ancient accounts do not show him entering Egypt itself, so "the kingdom of the king of the south" is read as the Syrian territory the Ptolemies then held (so Collins). The text gives no names.

a: He will take their gods to Egypt as prisoners
p: Taking a defeated people's gods was a sign of victory. Jerome says Egypt's own gods came home this way.
b: In the ancient world a victor often carried off the statues of the losers' gods (compare 1 Samuel 5:1-2; Jeremiah 48:7; 49:3). Jerome, following Porphyry, says Ptolemy III brought back to Egypt statues of gods that Cambyses had taken to Persia, and that Egyptians therefore called him Euergetes, "benefactor". This is Jerome's report; he names no Egyptian source for it. The verse gives the Jewish reader an example of the empire clash from the viewpoint of those who were not among the contenders: gods and nations were pieces in the game.

a: flood the land and pass through
p: The Bible pictures an invading army as a flood. The same words are used of Antiochus IV later in the chapter.
b: "Overflow and pass through" (shatap va'avar) is the language of invasion in Isaiah 8:7-8, where the king of Assyria sweeps through Judah like a river. Daniel uses it three times for Seleucid armies (here, 11:22 and 11:40), and in 9:26 the end comes with a flood. The "one of them" who floods the land is Antiochus III the Great (223-187 BC); his brother Seleucus III had been murdered in 223 BC. The reading "his sons" is the marginal reading (Qere); the written text (Ketiv) has "his son". See the variant.
r: Isaiah 8:7-8; Isaiah 28:15; Daniel 9:26; Daniel 11:22; Daniel 11:40; Nahum 1:8

a: The king of the south will boil with rage
p: Ptolemy IV beat Antiochus III in a huge battle near Gaza, but did not finish the job.
b: The king of the south is Ptolemy IV Philopator (221-204 BC). At Raphia, near Gaza, in 217 BC his army, which Polybius (5.79) puts at about 70,000 foot soldiers and 5,000 horse, met Antiochus III's army of about 62,000 foot and 6,000 horse, and won. The "crowd" (hamon, "multitude") handed over to him is the defeated Seleucid army. "His heart will swell with pride" fits the report that Ptolemy made a peace and went home rather than recover all Syria; he is said to have visited Jerusalem and tried to enter the Holy of Holies, a story told in 3 Maccabees 1-2, a book the Orthodox churches count as Scripture and other churches do not.

a: Men of violence from your own people
p: Some Jews took part in the wars. The text does not say who these men were or which vision they tried to fulfill.
b: The Hebrew says "sons of the violent ones (peritsim) of your people." Antiochus III took Judea from Egypt about 200 BC, and Josephus says the Jews welcomed him and helped him besiege the Egyptian garrison in the citadel (Antiquities 12.3.3). Some commentators think the phrase means pro-Seleucid Jews; others a rebel group; the "vision" they wanted to fulfill might be a prophecy of freedom such as Ezekiel 37 or Isaiah 11. The text calls them violent and says they will stumble, so it does not approve of their plan. The Greek (Theodotion) reads "the sons of the rest of your people." The text does not name the group.

a: take that walled city
p: Antiochus III wins Syria and Judea from Egypt. The fortified city is probably Sidon.
b: Antiochus III defeated the Egyptian general Scopas at Panium, near the sources of the Jordan, about 200 BC (some date the battle to 198). Scopas retreated to Sidon, where, after a siege and "a mound" (siege ramp), he surrendered about 198 BC. Egypt's "picked troops" could not break the siege. The result was that Judea, held by the Ptolemies for a century, passed to the Seleucids. The writer treats Judea as a prize caught in other men's wars.

a: the Beautiful Land
p: A name for Judah that Daniel uses four times. It is the Hebrew for "gazelle," "beauty" or "glory."
b: The Hebrew ha-tsevi means "the beauty" or "the glory" (also "gazelle"). It stands for the land of Israel in Daniel 8:9; 11:16, 41 and for the holy mountain in 11:45, and Jeremiah and Ezekiel use the same word for Israel's land as the most beautiful of all lands (Jeremiah 3:19; Ezekiel 20:6, 15). The Plain writes "the Beautiful Land" so the reader can follow the word and sees that the king of the north enters Judea three times in this chapter (11:16, 41, and the troops of 11:28-31).

a: He will offer him a young woman to be his wife
p: Antiochus III gave his daughter to Egypt's boy king about 193 BC, hoping to control Egypt. She took her husband's side.
b: Antiochus III arranged for his daughter Cleopatra I to marry Ptolemy V Epiphanes, probably in 194-193 BC, expecting to rule Egypt through her. She backed her husband, not her father, so "it will not work out for him." The Hebrew says "a daughter of the women," an odd idiom, probably "a young woman" or "a woman of the women's quarters." Ancient translators did not agree on the wording (see the variant on "a young woman"). Ptolemy V is "the king of the south" in the story and is the son of the Ptolemy IV of verse 11.

a: a commander will put a stop to the scorn he has shown
p: A Roman commander beat Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC.
b: After the marriage Antiochus III turned to the coastlands, the Aegean coast and Greece, and took many places (197-192 BC). Rome answered. At the battle of Magnesia in 190 BC the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with his brother Scipio Africanus, defeated him, and at the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BC he gave up Asia Minor west of the Taurus and paid a huge sum. The "commander" (qatsin) is the Roman, who turned back the Seleucid king's insults on his own head. Livy tells the story (books 37-38). This is the first appearance of Rome in the chapter, and the writer sees it only as an obstacle to the north.

a: he will vanish
p: He died in 187 BC while plundering a temple in Elam.
b: The same phrase, "he will fall and not be found," is used of the wicked in Psalm 37:36. Antiochus III, short of money after paying Rome, was killed in 187 BC in Elymais (ancient Elam) while trying to plunder a temple of Bel, according to ancient writers such as Diodorus Siculus and Strabo. The idea of a king dying in a pagan temple he tried to rob returns in the story of his son Antiochus IV (1 Maccabees 6:1-4).

a: sends a taskmaster through the glory of the kingdom
p: Seleucus IV needed money for Rome. His minister Heliodorus tried to take the Temple treasury.
b: Seleucus IV Philopator (187-175 BC) owed Rome heavy payments. His minister Heliodorus ("the taskmaster," noges) went to Jerusalem to take the Temple's money, a story told in 2 Maccabees 3. "The glory of the kingdom" is probably Judea and the Temple. The king was "broken" soon after the event, "not in anger and not in battle," that is, he was killed quietly. Appian says Heliodorus murdered him in 175 BC. The Hebrew word noges is used for Egyptian slave-drivers in Exodus 3:7; 5:6, and its verb is used for exacting tribute in 2 Kings 23:35; the Plain keeps "taskmaster" for the harsher word.

a: a despicable man
p: From here to 11:35 the angel describes Antiochus IV, who ruled 175-164 BC.
b: The Hebrew nivzeh means "despised" or "worthless." It is a play on the king's title Epiphanes ("God made visible"); Polybius reports that people called him Epimanes, "madman" (26.1). Seleucus IV's rightful heir was away as a hostage in Rome, and Antiochus IV, Seleucus' brother, took the throne with help from Eumenes of Pergamon and others, by "slippery" (chalaqlaqot, smooth) means rather than by inheritance. The rest of the chapter to verse 35 fits his life very closely, which is why most critical scholars and many conservative ones think Daniel 8 and 11 were written for the crisis he caused. See Daniel 8:9-14, 23-25; 1 Maccabees 1:10-64; 2 Maccabees 4-6.

a: a ruler of the covenant
t: Who is "a ruler of the covenant"?
p: Probably Onias III, the high priest, but Jerome (following Porphyry) names Ptolemy VI.
b: The Hebrew is nagid berit, "a ruler of a covenant." Most scholars (Collins, Goldingay) think this is the high priest Onias III, who was deposed in 175 BC when his brother Jason bought the office, and murdered about 171 BC (2 Maccabees 4:7-10, 30-38). The "covenant" would be the Jewish covenant with God, as in 11:28-32. Jerome, who reports Porphyry's reading, takes it to be the Egyptian king Ptolemy VI, the "covenant" an alliance with Antiochus. The Greek (Theodotion) has "a leader of the covenant."

a: he will hand out loot, plunder and property to his men
p: Antiochus IV was known for large gifts and shows of wealth.
b: Ancient writers report that Antiochus IV gave lavish gifts and held huge festivals; Polybius describes the games at Daphne (166 BC). 1 Maccabees 3:30 says he gave more generously than earlier kings. The line "what his fathers never did" refers to this. "He will plot against the fortresses, but only for a time" means his rise will not last.

a: The king of the south will prepare for battle
t: The first campaign in Egypt, 170 BC
p: Antiochus IV invaded Egypt, defeated the army of Ptolemy VI, and the king's own advisers betrayed him.
b: The Sixth Syrian War began in 170 BC when the advisers of the boy king Ptolemy VI Philometor, Eulaeus and Lenaeus, tried to retake Syria. Antiochus IV, Ptolemy's uncle, struck first, defeated the Egyptian army near Pelusium and took the young king into his keeping. "Those who eat his royal food" are the king's own table companions and advisers; their plotting is what "broke" him (11:26). 1 Maccabees 1:16-19 tells the same campaign from the Jewish side.

a: Across one table they will speak falsehood
p: Uncle and nephew, Antiochus IV and Ptolemy VI, met as allies and both lied.
b: Antiochus held his nephew Ptolemy VI, and the two met as allies, each lying: Antiochus claimed to be protecting his nephew, while Ptolemy was in his power. Their lies did not work, because Ptolemy's younger brother was crowned in Alexandria, so the plan to take Egypt failed. The writer's point: "the end still waits for the time set for it", the story is under God's schedule, not the kings'.

a: his heart will rise against the holy covenant
p: On the way home from Egypt Antiochus IV entered Jerusalem and took the Temple's treasures.
b: After his first Egyptian campaign Antiochus returned through Judea in 169 BC. 1 Maccabees 1:20-24 and 2 Maccabees 5:11-21 say he entered the sanctuary, took the gold altar, the lampstand, the table and the Temple's treasures, and killed many people. "The holy covenant" (berit qodesh) is the covenant between God and Israel, with the Law given at Sinai. Here the speech turns from kings' politics to the Temple. Everything after this verse concerns the people of the covenant.

a: his courage will break
p: A single Roman envoy stopped Antiochus IV at the gates of Alexandria. Antiochus turned his anger on Jerusalem.
b: In the spring of 168 BC Antiochus IV marched on Alexandria a second time. At Eleusis, a suburb, the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas gave him a Senate order to leave Egypt. When Antiochus asked for time, Popillius drew a circle round him in the sand with his staff and told him to answer before stepping out of it. Antiochus withdrew. Polybius (29.27) and Livy (45.12) tell the story. Rome had just won at Pydna (168 BC). Antiochus' humiliation is the background to the cruelty that follows: he went home through Judea (verse 30b) and started the persecution (167 BC). The Hebrew nikah means "be crushed" or "be disheartened."

a: Ships from Kittim
p: The name began as Cyprus. In Daniel it means the Roman fleet; the Greek simply says "Romans."
b: Kittim comes from Kition, a city on Cyprus. Genesis 10:4 lists Kittim among the sons of Javan (Greece). In Numbers 24:24, "ships from Kittim" humble Assyria and Eber, a phrase Daniel borrows. By this time the name had come to mean the lands and powers of the western Mediterranean. In 1 Maccabees 1:1 Alexander comes from the "land of Kittim" (Macedon), and in 8:5 Perseus is "king of Kittim." Here Kittim is Rome, as the Greek (Old Greek) says outright ("Romans") and as Jerome's Latin does. The Dead Sea Scrolls (the Pesher on Habakkuk, the War Scroll) use "Kittim" for the Romans, and so does Rashi: Rashi on 11:30 glosses it "Romans, troops from the kingdom of Rome." Moderns agree.

a: defile the sanctuary
t: The Temple is profaned, December 167 BC
p: Antiochus' decree of 167 BC banned the Jewish religion and turned the Temple into a pagan shrine.
b: In 167 BC Antiochus sent officers to enforce a decree against circumcision, the Sabbath, the food laws and the Law itself (1 Maccabees 1:41-64; 2 Maccabees 6:1-11). On 15 Kislev (December 167) an "abomination of desolation" was built on the altar, and on 25 Kislev sacrifice began on it (1 Maccabees 1:54, 59). 2 Maccabees 6:2 says the Temple was given to Olympian Zeus. Josephus adds that pigs were offered on the altar (Antiquities 12.5.4). "The fortress" (ha-ma'oz) is a second name for the sanctuary, which was strongly built; the Old Greek has "the holy place of fear."
r: 1 Maccabees 1:41-64; 2 Maccabees 6:1-11; Daniel 8:11-13; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 12:11; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14

a: the regular offering
p: The twice-daily sacrifice that never stopped. Its removal is the sign of the crisis in Daniel.
b: The tamid ("always, regular") was the lamb offered every morning and evening on the Temple altar (Exodus 29:38-42; Numbers 28:3-8). Daniel 8:11-13 first says the little horn took it away; 11:31 and 12:11 repeat it. 1 Maccabees 1:45 lists stopping "burnt offerings, sacrifice and drink offering" among Antiochus' decrees. The Mishnah (Tamid) and the Talmud treat it as the center of Temple worship. The Plain renders it "the regular offering," as in 8:11-13; the Greek calls it a "continual" offering.

a: the abomination that desolates
p: The Hebrew differs in each of Daniel's four passages. Matthew and Mark quote the Greek rendering.
b: Hebrew hashiqquts meshomem (11:31) is "the detestable thing," with the article, and meshomem, a participle meaning "that desolates." The other passages are related, not identical. In 12:11 the Hebrew is shiqquts shomem, with no article and a different participle form. In 9:27 it is kenaf shiqqutsim meshomem, "on a wing of abominations comes one who makes desolate": the noun is plural and the participle names a person, so the Plain of 9:27 keeps "abominations" and "one who makes desolate." In 8:13 it is hapesha' shomem, "the rebellion that desolates," with pesha' (rebellion), not shiqquts. Matthew 24:15 (site Plain: "the abomination of desolation") and Mark 13:14 quote the Greek rendering of Daniel, to bdelygma tes eremoseos. 1 Maccabees 1:54 has bdelygma eremoseos, without the article. Theodotion's Greek of 11:31 differs (see the variant).

a: set up
t: Why "abomination"? A sound-play on "Lord of heaven"
p: Many scholars hear a mocking twist on the Syrian title "Lord of heaven," the name of Zeus Olympios.
b: Many scholars (Nestle, Bickerman and Collins, among others) think the name is a deliberate twist on ba'al shamem, "Lord of heaven," the Syrian name for Zeus Olympios: shiqquts ("detestable") replaces ba'al, and shamem sounds like meshomem. Whether the thing was an altar, a statue, or a sacrifice on the altar (1 Maccabees 1:54, 59) is debated. Jesus speaks of Daniel's phrase as something still to come when he spoke (Matthew 24:15); the topic page follows the reading through the New Testament.

a: Those who act wickedly against the covenant
p: Some Jews gave up the covenant for the new customs. The text calls them wicked and says they were won over by words.
b: 1 Maccabees 1:11-15 tells how "renegades" asked permission to follow the practices of the nations, built a gymnasium in Jerusalem and "turned away from the holy covenant." 2 Maccabees 4 blames the high priests Jason and Menelaus. Daniel's word is mareshi'ei berit, "those who make the covenant wicked" (or "who act wickedly against it"). The Plain takes "corrupt" for yachanif, "make godless" or "flatter" (compare Numbers 35:33, "pollute"). "The people who know their God" are the ones who held firm, as the next verse describes.

a: Those among the people who have insight
p: The teachers of the people. The same word names the shining ones of 12:3. They may be the writers of Daniel.
b: Hebrew maskilim comes from sakal, "act wisely, understand." Daniel 1:4, 17 uses the verb of the young men's training, and 9:22 of Gabriel giving "insight." Here the maskilim "give understanding" (yavinu) to the many. The same two words, in Isaiah 52:13 and 53:11, describe the Servant who "succeeds" and "puts the many in the right." Several scholars (Collins and others) hold that the author of Daniel saw himself and his circle as sharing the Servant's work. If the book was written about 165 BC, these teachers are its authors and first readers; if in the sixth century, they are a future group the angel foresees. Daniel 12:3 and 12:10 describe the same group at the end.

a: a small help will come to them
p: Many take it as the Maccabean revolt, which the writer mentions without praise. Others say it is some other relief.
b: The "little help" and the many who "attach themselves to them with slippery words" are read in three ways. (1) The Maccabean uprising that began in 167-166 BC under Mattathias and Judas (1 Maccabees 2-4): the author counts it only a "little" help, and warns that many who joined were insincere. Critics take this as a sign that the book's author did not belong to the Maccabean party. (2) The Hasideans, who joined the revolt for a time (1 Maccabees 2:42). (3) Conservative readers who date Daniel to the sixth century read it as the same events as prophecy, or as help God sends in any persecution. Readers who think the whole book is a Maccabean-era work usually choose (1).

a: the time of the end
p: A set phrase in Daniel. What it ends is debated: Antiochus' persecution, or the age.
b: 'et qets, "time of the end," appears in Daniel 8:17, 11:35, 11:40, 12:4 and 12:9. Whether the "end" is the end of Antiochus' persecution in 164 BC, the end of the age, or both is the main dividing line between readings. Critical scholars read the end of the period of wrath (compare 8:19, "the end of the time of fury"); many Jewish and Christian interpreters read the end of the world; others see the first as a pattern for the second. Notice that "still for the time set" says the end has not yet come in the story. The Plain says "the time of the end" everywhere.

a: This king will follow his own will
p: The story changes here. Readers disagree whether it still describes Antiochus IV.
b: From 11:36 the speech names "the king" with no new name. There are four main readings. (1) Still Antiochus IV: Porphyry's reading, which Jerome reports, and the view of most critical scholars. He claimed divine honors, and 2 Maccabees 9:12 has him confess that no mortal should think himself equal to God. But verses 40-45 do not match what we know of his death (see the note there). (2) The Antichrist: Jerome says Christian writers apply it to the Antichrist, with Antiochus as his type; this is the view of dispensational readers (Pentecost) and many others. (3) Rome: Rashi explains it as "the kingdom of Rome". (4) A later power, such as the papacy for Isaac Newton and other historicists. The Plain does not choose.
r: Daniel 7:8; Daniel 7:25; Daniel 8:25; 2 Thessalonians 2:4; 2 Maccabees 9:12; Isaiah 14:13-14; Ezekiel 28:2

a: the desire of women
p: The Hebrew just says "the desire of women." Who or what that is, is debated: a god, a goddess, or a person.
b: chemdat nashim is unexplained. Suggestions: (1) the Syrian god Tammuz-Adonis, whom women mourned (Ezekiel 8:14) - Collins and others; (2) a goddess whom women honored, perhaps Nanaia or Anaitis, in whose temple at Elymais Antiochus IV died according to 2 Maccabees 1:13-16; (3) a king's own passion for women (an older view); (4) the Messiah, whom Jewish women hoped to bear: a reading some Christian commentators have offered. Antiochus did favor Zeus Olympios and issued coins bearing his own name and god-titles, which is what "no god of his fathers" would fit.

a: a god of fortresses
p: Perhaps Zeus Olympios or Jupiter Capitolinus. The Greek leaves the word untranslated.
b: The Hebrew 'eloah ma'uzzim means "a god of strongholds" or "of fortresses." Theodotion keeps the word in Greek letters (maozein), which shows that the translator did not understand it either. Proposals include Zeus Olympios (the god of the Temple's renaming, 2 Maccabees 6:2), Jupiter Capitolinus (the god of the Roman Capitol); Antiochus also worked on the great temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens (Livy 41.20). "A god his fathers did not know" is then a god the Seleucids had not honored before, or the king's own image. This is one of the least certain phrases in the chapter.

a: the king of the south will lock horns with him
t: Who fights whom at the end?
p: The verse has two kings and a pronoun "him". Readers disagree about who is meant.
b: The Hebrew uses "the king" (11:36) for the main figure, and then brings in "the king of the south" and "the king of the north" again; "him" in the first half and "him" in the second can refer to the same or to different people. Most readers take the willful king (11:36) as the actor, with the king of the south attacking him and the king of the north storming against him, or else take "the king of the north" as that same king. The text then lists countries he floods. The whole scene looks like Antiochus' campaigns of 170-168 BC on the surface, but only in outline, and the finish (11:44-45) does not match. Futurist readers see a coalition at the end of the age.

a: Edom, Moab and the best of the Ammonites
t: The nations east of the Jordan
p: Three old enemies of Israel are spared. The text does not say why.
b: Edom, Moab and Ammon were Israel's oldest eastern neighbors (Isaiah 11:14; Jeremiah 48-49). Edom, Moab and Ammon lie east and south-east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. A king marching from Syria to Egypt along the coast would leave them off to his east, which is one reason given for why he spares them; some think they are named as allies of the invader. Others find an echo of Isaiah 11:14 or Obadiah. In the second century BC Judas Maccabeus fought Edomites and Ammonites (1 Maccabees 5:3-8), so the nations were still enemies of Judah. The Qumran War Scroll lists the same three as foes of the sons of light (1QM I, 1-2). The Plain says "the best" for reshit, "the first," which can also be "the chief" or "the beginning."

a: Libyans and Cushites
p: North Africans fight in the king's army. Egyptian kings used the same troops.
b: Libyans (lubim) and Cushites (kushim, from the Nile south of Egypt) were soldiers in Egyptian armies (2 Chronicles 12:3; 16:8; Nahum 3:9). Here they march behind the invader, "at his heels" (literally "in his steps"). The Greek renders them Libyans and Ethiopians. Antiochus IV did not rule these lands, which is another reason scholars see 11:40-45 as no longer a record of known events.

a: the tents of his palace
t: A Persian word for a palace
p: 'Apadno is a Persian loanword. It occurs only here in the Bible.
b: 'apadno comes from Old Persian apadana, "palace" or "audience hall" (the great pillared hall at Persepolis and Susa is called an apadana). It occurs only here in the Bible. The writer uses a Persian word for a Hellenistic king's headquarters; Persian loanwords are a commonly cited feature of the book's language. Theodotion's Greek writes it in Greek letters (Ephadano). The Plain says "the tents of his palace," for the Hebrew "the tents of his apadana."

a: between the seas and the holy mountain of beauty
p: A site between the Mediterranean and Zion is not where Antiochus died. Readers take this three ways.
b: The Hebrew is "between the seas to the mountain of the beauty of holiness". "The seas" (plural) are most likely the Mediterranean (and perhaps the Dead Sea), and the holy mountain is Zion (Psalm 48:1; Isaiah 11:9). Antiochus IV died far away in Persia in 164 BC, according to 1 Maccabees 6:1-16 and Polybius (31.9), who place his death at Tabae. So readers differ: (1) the author expected a death in Judea and was wrong (Collins); (2) the verses describe an end-time figure, not Antiochus (Jerome and the futurist tradition); (3) "the seas" and "the mountain" are symbols of the nations and God's people. The Old Greek says "between the seas and the mountain of the desire of the holy one."
r: Psalm 48:1; Isaiah 11:9; Ezekiel 38:14-16; Joel 2:20; 1 Maccabees 6:1-16; 2 Maccabees 9:1-29

a: His end will come, and he will have no helper
p: The end of the tyrant is told in the words that end other prophecies of his kind.
b: Prophets end the story of a tyrant with his death and with no one to help (Isaiah 14:19-20; Ezekiel 28:19; Ezekiel 39:4). In 8:25 the same figure is broken without human hands, and in 7:26 his rule is taken away at the judgment. The Hebrew is ad qitso, "to his end." On the Antiochus reading it is the king's own end; on the futurist reading it is the end of the last king at the end of the age. The writers of Revelation read the figure's fall as the pattern for the beast's (Revelation 19:19-21).

a: Michael will stand up
p: Michael is the heavenly guardian of Israel. Daniel 10 shows him fighting the angelic princes of Persia and Greece.
b: Michael is named in Daniel 10:13, 21 and here. His name means "Who is like God?" In Daniel he is "one of the chief princes", the "prince" of Israel, set against the princes of Persia and Greece. "Stands guard over the sons of your people" is the work of an advocate in court. Jude 9 and Revelation 12:7 name him as the angel who fights Satan and the dragon. In 1 Enoch 9:1 and 20:5 he is one of the four or seven archangels, set over the people; the War Scroll from Qumran calls on his help in the final battle. The Catholic Catechism and the Orthodox calendar of feasts treat him as an archangel, and the Jehovah's Witnesses and Adventist writers identify him with Christ. Calvin leaves both readings open, and Matthew Henry reads the "great prince" of 12:1 as Christ (see the "Where Christians differ" card). The topic page Michael follows him through the Bible.
r: Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:21; Jude 9; Revelation 12:7; 1 Enoch 9:1; 1 Enoch 20:5

a: A time of distress will come, with no equal
p: Jeremiah, Joel and Jesus all use this language of an unmatched disaster.
b: Jeremiah 30:7 says of the day of Jacob's trouble that there is none like it, and promises that Jacob will be saved out of it. Joel 2:2 uses the words of the day of the LORD. Jesus applies Daniel's wording to the days around Jerusalem's fall (Matthew 24:21; Mark 13:19), and Revelation 7:14 speaks of those "coming out of the great suffering" and 16:18 of an earthquake with no equal. The Maccabean reading ties the trouble to 167-164 BC; the Jewish and Christian tradition mostly sees it as the last tribulation (see the topic page The Great Tribulation). Preterists read it as the Roman war of AD 66-70.
r: Jeremiah 30:7; Joel 2:2; Matthew 24:21; Mark 13:19; Revelation 7:14; Revelation 16:18

a: everyone found written in the scroll
p: God keeps a record of his people. Being "written" means belonging to those who will be rescued.
b: The idea of a heavenly record of names is old: Moses asks to be wiped from God's book (Exodus 32:32), the psalmist asks that his enemies be wiped from "the scroll of life" (Psalm 69:28), and Isaiah 4:3 speaks of everyone written down for life in Jerusalem. Malachi 3:16 has a "scroll of remembrance." In Daniel 7:10 "books were opened" in the court. Here the scroll lists those who will escape the time of trouble, and 12:2 leads on to those who rise. Revelation makes the scroll the "book of life" (Revelation 3:5; 20:12, 15; 21:27). The Plain says "scroll" as in Psalm 69:28.
r: Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Isaiah 4:3; Malachi 3:16; Daniel 7:10; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 20:15

a: Many of those asleep in the dusty ground will wake up
t: The clearest resurrection verse in the Hebrew Bible
p: Read as bodily resurrection by most Jews and Christians; some critics limit it to the persecution's martyrs and traitors.
b: Earlier texts pictured death as the end (Job 14:12) or spoke of national revival (Hosea 6:1-2; Ezekiel 37) or of a hope for the faithful (Isaiah 26:19). Daniel 12:2 is the first text most scholars agree clearly speaks of individuals waking from the dust to different fates. Views: (1) A bodily resurrection of the dead at the end, the main Jewish and Christian reading (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 makes belief in it a test; Rashi says "The dead will come to life"; Jesus in John 5:28-29; Paul in Acts 24:15). (2) A limited resurrection: only "many", the exceptionally righteous martyrs and exceptionally wicked traitors of the persecution (Collins, Nickelsburg). (3) A picture of national restoration in the style of Ezekiel 37, a view held by some older critics. "Asleep" is a common Bible word for the dead; the verse uses it itself, and compare Job 14:12 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13. (Daniel 12:13 says "rest," tanuach, not "sleep.")
r: Isaiah 26:19; Ezekiel 37:1-14; Hosea 6:1-2; John 5:28-29; Acts 24:15; Matthew 25:46; 2 Maccabees 7:9

a: the dusty ground
p: A phrase that echoes Genesis 3:19. And "many" is the same word as in Isaiah 53, meaning "the many" in a wide sense.
b: Literally "the ground of dust" (admat afar): the grave, and a reminder of Genesis 3:19, "to dust you will go back", with Isaiah 26:19, "you who lie in the dust." Rabbim, "many," is not a limit: in a Semitic idiom "the many" can mean the great mass, all the people, as in Isaiah 53:11-12 (compare Romans 5:15, 19, where Paul sets "the many" beside "all"). So "many of those asleep" is read by many Jewish and Christian interpreters as a way of saying "those asleep, a great multitude" and not "some". The question stays open, and the Plain says "many".
orig: רַבִּים מִיְּשֵׁנֵי אַדְמַת עָפָר (rabbim miyeshenei admat afar)

a: a horror without end
p: The word used here appears in only one other place in the Bible, Isaiah 66:24, in the same Plain wording.
b: Dera'on occurs only here and in Isaiah 66:24, where the dead bodies of the rebels are "a horror to all flesh". It means something that makes people shrink away, and it is paired here with "shame" (cherpot, "reproaches, disgrace"). The Plain follows Isaiah. Whether this is an endless conscious punishment, a state of ruin that ends in destruction, or a separation, is the main difference between the churches' teaching (see the card). The Hebrew says only that the "horror" has no end.

a: Those with insight will gleam
p: Daniel 12:3 uses two words from Isaiah's Suffering Servant: "succeed" and "make righteous the many."
b: Isaiah 52:13 says the Servant yaskil, "will prosper" or "act with insight", and 53:11 says he yatsdiq rabbim, "will put the many in the right". Daniel 12:3 puts the two roots side by side: the maskilim ("insightful") and matsdiqei harabbim ("those who put the many in the right"). Scholars such as Collins have argued that the author saw the teachers and martyrs of his own time as sharing the Servant's work. If so, those who die in the persecution (11:33-35) are not lost: their faithfulness becomes the reason for others' righteousness, and they shine. The Plain uses Isaiah 53:11's wording for the second line.

a: will blaze like the stars
p: Stars often stand for angels. The verse promises the faithful a place among them, or at least their brightness.
b: In the Bible the stars are God's heavenly court (Job 38:7), and in Daniel 8:10 "stars" are the holy people thrown down. 1 Enoch 104:2 promises the righteous that they will shine like the lights of heaven, and Wisdom 3:7 says the righteous will shine forth. Jesus says the righteous will "blaze out like the sun" (Matthew 13:43). Some readers take Daniel 12:3 as a simile only, and others, from 1 Enoch to Paul's "glory" of the body (1 Corinthians 15:40-41), hear a real change into an angel-like state. The Plain uses "gleam" for yazhiru and "blaze" for the stars so the two lines are heard separately.
r: Job 38:7; Daniel 8:10; Matthew 13:43; 1 Corinthians 15:40-41; 1 Enoch 104:2; Wisdom 3:7

a: seal the scroll
p: In Daniel a sealed book waits for its time. In Revelation the seal is opened.
b: Sealing a scroll kept it private and certified it (Isaiah 8:16; 29:11; Jeremiah 32:10-14). Here Daniel is told to seal the book until the end, because the vision concerns a later time (8:26). Revelation 5:1 shows a sealed scroll opened by the Lamb, and Revelation 22:10 tells John not to seal, because the time is near. If the book was written about 165 BC, "seal" is the author's way of explaining why a sixth-century prophet's words appeared only then; traditional readers take it as a command that kept the book hidden for centuries. Hebrew satam ("stop up, keep closed") and chatam ("seal") appear together.

a: rove around
t: "Run to and fro" is not about travel
p: The verse does not predict faster travel or more science. The Hebrew says people will roam, and the knowledge is disputed.
b: The KJV's "many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased" has been taken as a prophecy of cars, planes or the internet. The Hebrew verb shut means to roam or wander, searching (Jeremiah 5:1; Amos 8:12; Zechariah 4:10). Amos 8:12 pictures people roaming in search of God's word and not finding it, which suggests that Daniel's "many will rove around" is a search for understanding (so Collins) and not an increase of travel. The Hebrew ha-da'at "the knowledge" may be the knowledge of the book's meaning. The Greek has a different text (see the variant), and some scholars think the Old Greek's translator read ra'ah, "evil," for da'at, "knowledge."
orig: יְשֹׁטְטוּ רַבִּים וְתִרְבֶּה הַדָּעַת (yeshotetu rabbim vetirbeh hada'at)

a: the man in linen clothes
p: He is the figure of Daniel 10:5-6, and one who also appears in Ezekiel as a scribe.
b: Daniel 10:5-6 describes the man in linen with a belt of gold, a body like beryl and a face like lightning. Ezekiel 9:2-3, 11 has a man in linen with a writing case who marks the faithful in Jerusalem, and Revelation 1:13 has "one like a son of man" in a long robe. Readers identify him as Gabriel, an unnamed angel, or (in many Christian readings of chapter 10) the Son of God before his birth. In 12:5-7 he is above the water of the river, and one of the two others asks him the question. The Hebrew does not say what his place above the water means. The Plain says "in linen clothes" to match 10:5.

a: How long until the wonders come to their end
p: The question of the sufferers throughout the Bible, from Psalms to Revelation.
b: "How long?" (ad matai) is the cry of the Psalms (Psalm 74:10; 79:5; 90:13), of Isaiah (Isaiah 6:11) and of the angel in Zechariah 1:12. The martyrs under the altar ask it in Revelation 6:10. Here two angels ask it for Daniel, and the answer in verse 7 is the oath. The book that began with exiles (1:1-2) ends with the same question the exiles asked.

a: He raised his right hand and his left hand
p: An oath by God was usually sworn with one hand raised. Two hands make this oath exceptional.
b: Deuteronomy 32:40 has God lift one hand and swear "As I live forever." Revelation 10:5-6 reuses this oath for the angel (the Plain there says "lifted his right hand"). Daniel's angel lifts both hands and swears "by the one who lives forever", a title from Daniel 4:34. The doubled gesture underlines how binding the oath is. The oath is also an answer: the delay has a fixed length.

a: a time, times and half a time
t: "A time, times and half a time"
p: The same phrase as 7:25. It most likely means three and a half years. The Maccabean persecution was about that long.
b: Mo'ed mo'adim va-chetsi, "an appointed time, appointed times and a half," is also found in Daniel 7:25 (Aramaic). Revelation rewrites it as 42 months and 1,260 days (Revelation 11:2-3; 12:6, 14; 13:5). Readings: (1) Three and a half years (a "time" is a year, "times" two): the length of Antiochus' persecution, 167-164 BC, as counted in round numbers. (2) A broken seven: half of the perfect number, a limited time of trouble. (3) Year-days: 1,260 years, in the historicist tradition (Newton; the Adventist reading of AD 538 to 1798 in The Great Controversy). (4) Half of the last seven years, the second half of the tribulation in the dispensationalist reading of 9:27. See the topic page.

a: could not grasp it
p: A prophet who writes down what he cannot explain.
b: Daniel is again unable to follow the vision (8:27; 12:8), and asks about the "outcome" (acharit), the final end. He is told not to ask, because the words are sealed. Zechariah has the same exchange: "I do not know, my lord" (Zechariah 4:5, 13). First Peter 1:10-12 says that the prophets "searched" for the time and meaning of what they wrote and were told it was for a later generation. For critical readers, the line also fits an author who has to explain why an old prophet's words only now make sense.

a: purge themselves, whiten themselves and be refined
p: The same three verbs as 11:35. The suffering of the faithful is described as a refining process.
b: The three verbs barar (purge), laban (make white) and tsaraf (refine) are used together in 11:35 and 12:10. Silver is refined in fire (Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:2-3), and sin is "made white as snow" (Isaiah 1:18; Psalm 51:7). Revelation 7:14 has the multitude wash their robes and make them white. 11:35 says God refines "some" of the insightful by letting them stumble; 12:10 says "many" cleanse themselves, so the suffering has a purpose. The line "none of the wicked will understand, but those with insight will understand" is a wisdom saying (Hosea 14:9).
r: Daniel 11:35; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:2-3; Isaiah 1:18; Psalm 51:7; Hosea 14:9; Revelation 7:14

a: 1,290 days
p: Daniel gives four numbers for the crisis. Different readers explain them differently.
b: Daniel gives 2,300 "evenings and mornings" (8:14), "a time, times and half a time" (7:25; 12:7), 1,290 days (12:11) and 1,335 days (12:12). The arithmetic is 1,260 + 30 = 1,290, and 1,290 + 45 = 1,335. Maccabean reading: the Temple was defiled on 15 Kislev 167 BC and rededicated on 25 Kislev 164 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52), about 1,100 days. Many critics think the larger numbers were added when the end did not come in the expected time (so Collins, and others). Porphyry, as Jerome reports him, tied the 1,290 to Antiochus and the extra 45 to the Maccabean victory. Year-day reading: days stand for years (Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6), as in Newton and the Adventist tradition. Jewish reading: Rashi links the 1,290 to the 2,300 of 8:14 and counts to the days of the Messiah (as the Judaica Press translation on Sefaria gives it), while the Talmud warns against calculating the end (Sanhedrin 97b).
r: Daniel 7:25; Daniel 8:14; Daniel 12:7; Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 1 Maccabees 4:52

a: regular offering
t: Literal days, and the leap-month idea
p: Jerome counts literal days from the end of the offering. A leap-month idea for the extra 30 days does not fit the figures well.
b: Futurist reading: literal days. Jerome, who rejects Porphyry here, takes the 1,290 days as the persecution of the Antichrist, counted from the removal of the regular offering, which he gives as three and a half years or 1,290 days; he reads the further 45 days as a delay that tests the patience of the saints, for a reason known to God. Leap-month proposal: some popular expositions explain the extra 30 days as an intercalary month, which a lunar-solar calendar needs about every three years. The figures do not fit well: three and a half lunar years of 354 days come to about 1,239 days, or about 1,269 with one leap month, and no calendar rule accounts for the further 45 days.
r: Daniel 7:25; Daniel 8:14; Daniel 12:7; Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 1 Maccabees 4:52

a: 1,335 days
p: A blessing for those who endure past 1,290. It does not say what happens on day 1,335.
b: Daniel does not say what will happen at the end of the 1,335 days; the blessing is on those who wait and "arrive." Readers differ: the date of the Temple's rededication in 164 BC, some later event of deliverance in the Maccabean crisis, the coming of the kingdom, or the resurrection. The Hebrew word ashrei is the same as in Psalm 1:1, "blessed". Because each number moves the date further, Jewish tradition (b. Sanhedrin 97b) warned against working out the date of the end. First readers were meant to take comfort in waiting, not in a calendar.

a: You will rest, and you will rise
p: The book ends with a personal promise to Daniel: rest in death, and then a place in the end.
b: Verses 1-3 promised a resurrection for the people; verse 13 promises Daniel himself that he will "rest" (die) and then "rise" (ta'amod, "stand up") to his goral ("lot", a portion assigned by lot, as in Joshua 18:6 and Psalm 16:5). The book's final line is therefore a promise of resurrection, not an explanation of the numbers. Daniel is told to "go on to the end", which can be his own death or the end of the days. Jewish and Christian readers hear the promise as for every faithful person, and later tradition claims Daniel's tomb at Susa and several other places, which the text does not mention. The Greek has "to your glory" (see the variant).
